Title: GitHub workflow: own account, branch, pull request, review, and a check of our repository and board
User story: As a team member, I want to practise the GitHub workflow on my own account and check our team repository and board, so that all our later work is saved, reviewed and visible. (GitHub = a website where teams keep and share code. Repository = the project folder stored on GitHub. Branch = a separate copy of the work where you can try changes safely. Pull request = a request to add your changes to the main work so teammates can review them.)
Acceptance criteria:
1) A 5-line note and a small working example are saved in our "learning" folder.
2) I accepted the repository invite, can see the team board with all backlog items, and made one pull request that a teammate reviewed and merged.
3) I explained it in 3 minutes at the Friday help meeting.

Title: FastAPI hello world
User story: As a team member, I want to build a FastAPI hello world, so that I understand how our backend answers requests. (FastAPI = a Python tool for building the backend, the part that holds the logic and talks to the database. API = the way a web page asks the server for data.)
Acceptance criteria:
1) A 5-line note and a small working example are saved in our "learning" folder.
2) Opening the /hello address in a browser shows a message from my FastAPI program.
3) I explained it in 3 minutes at the Friday help meeting.

Title: Flutter and Dart hello world
User story: As a team member, I want to build a small Flutter app with one screen, a heading and a button that changes the text when tapped, so that I understand how the screens of our mobile app are made. (Flutter = a free toolkit for building mobile apps that run on phones. Dart = the programming language we use to write Flutter apps. Emulator = a pretend phone that runs on your laptop.)
Acceptance criteria:
1) A 5-line note and a small working example are saved in our "learning" folder.
2) The app runs on my emulator, on my phone or, as a fallback only, in the Chrome browser. It shows the heading, and the button changes the text when tapped.
3) I explained it in 3 minutes at the Friday help meeting.

Title: PostgreSQL basics
User story: As a team member, I want to create a table and save and read rows in PostgreSQL, so that I understand how our app stores data. (PostgreSQL = a free database, an organised place to store data. SQL = the language used to talk to a database.)
Acceptance criteria:
1) A 5-line note and a small working example are saved in our "learning" folder.
2) I created a "tasks" table, saved 3 rows and read them back with SQL.
3) I explained it in 3 minutes at the Friday help meeting.

Title: Docker basics
User story: As a team member, I want to run a small program in a Docker container, so that my code runs the same way on every teammate's laptop. (Docker = a tool that packs a program with everything it needs into a container.)
Acceptance criteria:
1) A 5-line note and a small working example are saved in our "learning" folder.
2) A hello container starts with one command and shows its message.
3) I explained it in 3 minutes at the Friday help meeting.

Title: pytest basics
User story: As a team member, I want to write simple automatic tests with pytest, so that I can check my code without testing by hand. (pytest = a Python tool that runs small test programs which check our code.)
Acceptance criteria:
1) A 5-line note and a small working example are saved in our "learning" folder.
2) I wrote 2 passing tests, and I showed one failing test and then fixed it.
3) I explained it in 3 minutes at the Friday help meeting.

Title: Password hashing basics (bcrypt or Argon2)
User story: As a team member, I want to hash and check a password in a small example, so that I understand how to store passwords safely. (Hashing = turning a password into a scrambled code that cannot be turned back. bcrypt and Argon2 = free tools that do this safely.)
Acceptance criteria:
1) A 5-line note and a small working example are saved in our "learning" folder.
2) My example accepts the right password and rejects a wrong one, and hashing the same password twice gives two different codes.
3) I explained it in 3 minutes at the Friday help meeting.

Title: Walking skeleton: one task from the Flutter app to the database and back
User story: As a user planning my week, I want to add one Personal task and see it on my screen, so that I know the app saves what I type. (A walking skeleton = the smallest version that works from start to finish. It is a first, simple path through the whole system.)
Acceptance criteria:
1) The Flutter app sends the task to the FastAPI backend and it is saved in PostgreSQL.
2) After I close and reopen the app, the saved task is still shown.
3) The whole thing starts with one documented command (Docker if the laptop can run it, otherwise a run script) and was merged by pull request.
Suggested sprint: 3 (may start in 2 if the learning finishes early)

Title: Sign-up and login with hashed passwords and login attempt limits
User story: As a user with Personal and Work tasks, I want to sign up and log in with a password, so that only I can see my tasks and events.
Acceptance criteria:
1) The database stores a hash, never the plain password.
2) After 5 wrong passwords in a row the account is locked for a short time.
3) A pytest test checks that a right password works and a wrong one fails.

Title: In-app calendar with the six categories and event status
User story: As a user with a full life, I want a calendar where each event has a category (Study, Work, Personal, Family, Health or Errands), so that I can see all of my life in one place.
Acceptance criteria:
1) I can add an event with a title, a time and one of the six categories.
2) The calendar shows each event with its category.
3) Each event stores whether it was kept, moved or missed.

Title: Security tools basics: TOTP multi-factor code, AES-256 encryption, HTTPS (one small example each)
User story: As a team member, I want to build one small example each of a TOTP code, AES-256 encryption and HTTPS, so that I understand the security tools we will use for login and for protecting stored data. (TOTP = a time-based one-time password: a 6-digit code from an authenticator app that changes after a short time. AES-256 = a strong way to lock (encrypt) data so that only a person with the key can read it. Key = the secret value used to lock and unlock data. HTTPS = the secure way an app talks to a server, so that others cannot read the messages. Environment variable = a setting kept on your laptop, outside the code.)
Acceptance criteria:
1) A 5-line note and one small working example each of a TOTP code, AES-256 encryption and HTTPS are saved in our "learning" folder.
2) The AES-256 example reads its key from an environment variable; the key is never written in the code, and a search of the code for the key text finds nothing.
3) I explained it in 3 minutes at the Friday help meeting.

Title: Multi-factor login with a TOTP code
User story: As a user with Personal and Work tasks, I want to enter a 6-digit code from an authenticator app after my password, so that nobody can open my account with only my password. (Multi-factor login = logging in with two proofs, here the password and a code. TOTP = a time-based one-time password: a code that an authenticator app makes and that changes after a short time. Authenticator app = a phone app that shows the code. pytest = a Python tool for running automatic tests.)
Acceptance criteria:
1) After the right password, a Flutter screen asks for the 6-digit code, and only a right code lets me in.
2) A wrong code is rejected and counts toward the same 5-try lock as wrong passwords.
3) A pytest test checks that a right code works and a wrong code fails.

Title: Calling an AI model through an API
User story: As a team member, I want our FastAPI backend to call an AI model through an API, so that our secretary and coach can answer questions without the app ever holding a secret key. (AI model = a program that writes answers to questions; we use the free option chosen in PB-37. API key = a secret password that lets our program use the AI service. Environment variable = a setting kept on your laptop, outside the code. .gitignore = a file that tells git which files never to save in the repository.)
Acceptance criteria:
1) The API key is read from an environment variable and is not in the repository: I showed the .gitignore line, and a search of the repository for the key text finds nothing.
2) A question sent to the FastAPI backend gets a reply from the AI model.
3) If the AI service fails or the free limit is reached, the user sees a friendly error message and not a crash.

Title: Coach prototype: step-by-step hints on about 20 sample questions, with a written go or no-go result
User story: As a student using Learn mode, I want the coach to give step-by-step hints before the full answer, so that I try to solve the problem myself and learn more. (Prototype = a first small version made to test an idea. Hint = a small clue that helps without giving the answer. Go or no-go = a decision to continue with the idea or to stop.)
Acceptance criteria:
1) 20 sample questions are saved in a file, and each has three steps of hints: a nudging question, a pointer to the idea, and a worked step.
2) The full answer comes only after three attempts, and a results table lists for each question: hints helped (yes/no) and full answer held back (yes/no).
3) A written go or no-go decision with a reason is saved in our "docs" folder.

Title: Every member has a working setup
User story: As a team member, I want my laptop to have all the tools we need installed and checked, so that I can start the learning items in Sprint 2 without losing time. (Git = the tool that records changes to code; a commit is one saved set of changes. Python = the programming language of our backend. Flutter SDK = the toolkit we install to build our mobile app; it includes the Dart language. flutter doctor = a Flutter command that checks if your setup is complete. Code editor = a program for writing code. Emulator = a pretend phone that runs on your laptop. pgAdmin = a free window for looking at a PostgreSQL database.)
Acceptance criteria:
1) git --version, python --version and flutter --version each show a version number, and I posted a screenshot of these and of the flutter doctor result in the team group.
2) My commits show my own name and GitHub email.
3) For PostgreSQL and Docker, either pgAdmin opens and docker --version works, or I told the team why my laptop cannot run them. I also said where I can run the Flutter hello app (emulator, phone, or Chrome as a fallback).

Title: Delete my data: a user can delete their account and all their data
User story: As a user with Family and Health events, I want to delete my account and all my data, so that nothing about my life stays stored if I stop using the app.
Acceptance criteria:
1) A "Delete my account" button asks for my password and then removes my account.
2) After deleting, my tasks, events and categories are no longer in the database (checked by looking in the database).
3) A pytest test shows that another user's data is still there.

Title: Private categories: a user can lock a category so other accounts cannot read it and it is never sent to the AI
User story: As a user with Health and Family events, I want to lock a category, so that other accounts cannot read it and its text is never sent to the AI.
Acceptance criteria:
1) I can lock and unlock any of the six categories.
2) A second test account cannot see the events in my locked category.
3) Text from a locked category is never sent to the AI (checked in the test log, using fake data).

Title: Report a bad answer button for the coach
User story: As a user studying for an exam, I want to report a bad coach answer with one click, so that wrong hints are found and fixed.
Acceptance criteria:
1) Every coach answer has a "Report a bad answer" button.
2) Clicking it saves the question, the answer and the time, with no personal details.
3) The team can see the list of reports.

Title: Export the calendar as a file
User story: As a user with a busy week, I want to download my calendar as a file, so that I can open it in another calendar app. (The usual calendar file type is called .ics.)
Acceptance criteria:
1) An "Export" button downloads a calendar file.
2) The file contains my events with their title, time and category.
3) The file opens without errors in one free calendar app that we test with.

Title: Protect the learning data from fake events: rate limits, outlier filter and a tampering test
User story: As a user who relies on time suggestions, I want protection against fake events that could mislead the learning, so that my suggestions stay trustworthy. (A rate limit = a limit on how many requests one account can make in a short time. An outlier = a value far away from all the others, such as 50 events at 3 a.m. A tampering test = a test where we try to fool our own app on purpose.)
Acceptance criteria:
1) One account cannot add more than 20 new events in one minute (the number is a guess the team can change).
2) The outlier filter ignores events that are far outside normal when the model learns.
3) A tampering test adds bulk fake events to a test account, and the suggestions change only a little (before and after are written down).

Title: Compare free AI options and choose one (cost check)
User story: As a team member, I want to compare free AI options and choose one, so that our coach and chat do not cost money and we know the limits before the Sprint 3 work needs them. (A free option usually has limits, such as how many questions you can ask per day.)
Acceptance criteria:
1) A 5-line note compares at least 3 free AI options (what is free, the limits, how private it is) and is saved in our "learning" folder.
2) The team chose one option and wrote the reason in one line, and one small test question got an answer from it.
3) I explained the choice in 3 minutes at the Friday help meeting.

Title: Dart and Flutter basics: screens, state, and calling our backend
User story: As a team member, I want to learn how a Flutter app shows screens, keeps state and calls our backend, so that I can build the real screens of our app and connect them to the FastAPI backend. (Dart = the programming language we use to write Flutter apps. Flutter = a free toolkit for building mobile apps. Screen = one page of the app that the user sees. State = the data a screen remembers and shows right now, so the screen changes when the data changes. HTTP = the way the app sends a request to the backend and gets a reply.)
Acceptance criteria:
1) A 5-line note and a small working example are saved in our "learning" folder.
2) A screen shows a list that updates when I add an item (this is "state").
3) The app calls the PB-02 /hello address over HTTP and shows the reply; I explained it in 3 minutes at the Friday help meeting.

Title: Architecture sketch, database tables and API list
User story: As a team member, I want one clear architecture sketch, a list of database tables and a list of API addresses, so that all six of us build parts that fit together. (Architecture = the plan that shows the main parts of a system and how they connect. Database table = a grid in the database that stores one kind of data, with a column for each detail. API address = an address the app calls to ask the backend to do something; each has a method, which is the kind of request, such as read or send. AI model = a program that writes answers to questions. AI key = the secret password for the AI service.)
Acceptance criteria:
1) A one-page picture shows how the Flutter app, the FastAPI backend, PostgreSQL and the AI model connect, and states that only the backend holds the AI key and database access.
2) A list of database tables (users, tasks, events) with their columns, and a list of API addresses (sign-up, login, tasks) with method, input and output.
3) One teammate reviewed it and the files are in our "docs" folder.
